description: Grupo perteneciente a compañeros del TECNM campus Zacatepec con el fin de realizar estudios competentes en astro física y cosmologia
summary:
SPHEREx Temporal Observatory is an interactive citizen science web platform designed to democratize the analysis of infrared data from NASA's SPHEREx mission, eliminating the need for programming skills. Faced with the challenge of inspecting over one billion astronomical sources observed every six months across 102 spectral bands (0.75 to 5.0 um), the system replaces complex manual workflows with an intuitive, publicly accessible visual environment.

Through automated astrophysical processing and temporal comparison between reprocessed observations (DR1 and QR3), the platform detects, classifies, and catalogs moving objects—such as asteroids, comets, brown dwarfs, and trans-Neptunian candidates (Planet X). To validate these findings with scientific rigor, it integrates three 3D visualization tools: Cosmic Sky (a volumetric celestial sphere), an Orbital and Parallax Simulator based on Earth's 2 AU baseline, and a 3D Spectral Cube that distinguishes true chemical signatures from instrumental noise or cosmic rays. As a result, SPHEREx Temporal Observatory enables researchers, students, and citizens to discover dynamic phenomena in the universe quickly, intuitively, and verifiably.
details:
The SPHEREx Temporal Observatory is an interactive citizen-science web platform that democratizes the exploration and analysis of infrared data from NASA’s SPHEREx mission, requiring no programming knowledge. SPHEREx observes over a billion astronomical sources every six months across 102 spectral bands (0.75 to 5.0 micrometers). To make this volume of data manageable, the platform replaces complex, manual astrophysical workflows with an intuitive, visual, and reproducible environment.

How it works and scientific architecture

The platform ingests actual scientific data products in FITS format (Level 2 spectral images with multiple extensions), verifies their integrity using SHA-256 checksums, and validates their astrometric calibration via World Coordinate Systems (WCS). Using this dataset, it automatically generates astronomical previews, extracts calibrated spectral profiles, and detects individual celestial sources. Throughout the process, it maintains full traceability back to the original file, including its associated uncertainties and quality indicators.

To enable users to rigorously validate findings without writing code, the platform integrates three interactive 3D environments:

Cosmic Sky: A volumetric celestial sphere for navigating real infrared maps and inspecting regions of the sky.

Orbital and Parallax Simulator: A model based on Earth’s orbital baseline (2 AU) for assessing the trajectories and distances of moving objects, such as asteroids, comets, brown dwarfs, and trans-Neptunian candidates.

3D Spectral Cube: A multispectral analysis tool that cross-references wavelength, variance, and quality masks to distinguish genuine chemical signatures from instrumental noise or cosmic rays. Benefits and Impact

The SPHEREx Temporal Observatory drastically lowers the technical barrier to accessing NASA’s infrared catalogs. Researchers, students, and astronomy enthusiasts can actively engage in investigating dynamic phenomena in the universe—quickly, visually, and in a scientifically verifiable manner.

Technology Stack

Backend and processing: Built in Python using FastAPI and Uvicorn, incorporating specialized astrophysics libraries for analyzing FITS files, performing WCS transformations, propagating uncertainties, and managing reproducible manifests.

Frontend and visualization: Developed using TypeScript, React, and Vite, featuring in-browser 3D rendering engines for seamless space exploration.

Quality and validation: Automated verification via Pytest test suites and static type checking.

Innovation and Team Approach

Unlike traditional tools reliant on static tables or command-line scripts, this observatory transforms 102-channel astronomical arrays into navigable spatial experiences. The team also prioritized scientific integrity and data transparency. When metadata or compatible multi-epoch observations are missing, the system never generates synthetic data or simulations to create the appearance of results. Instead, it explicitly highlights the limitations of each observation, prevents comparisons that lack documentary support, and ensures that every measurement remains auditable and reproducible.
